output:
*Interview with Rosa Häfeli, maid and cook, in the dining room. Second interview of the night.*

MATTHEY: Sit down, Mademoiselle Häfeli. You are not in any trouble. I want to hear about the kitchen tonight, and about the house, in your own words. Take your time.

ROSA: Ja, Monsieur. Herrgott, I have never sat in this room at night. Madame says the dining room is for guests.

MATTHEY: Begin with the kitchen.

ROSA: The kitchen is mine. I keep it the way my mother kept ours in the Emmental. Tonight I had the champagne glasses out for the toast. I washed them twice, because the master looks at everything, even glasses.

MATTHEY: You have a clock in the kitchen?

ROSA: On the shelf by the stove, an American alarm clock. It was cheap, but it keeps good time. My kitchen clock is a quarter of an hour fast. I keep it so on purpose, so nothing is ever late. The coffee is ready before Madame asks for it.

MATTHEY: You set it yourself?

ROSA: I did. I know exactly how far it is, a quarter of an hour, and I am never wrong about that. Madame has teased me about it for years. She says I live in the future.

MATTHEY: Tell me about Fräulein Lina.

ROSA: Fräulein Lina came down into the kitchen at thirteen minutes to eleven by my kitchen clock. She sat at my table and did not say much. She never says much. She is a farmer's daughter from Le Locle, they are like stones up there. She stayed with me until after the temple struck eleven.

MATTHEY: And the piano?

ROSA: We heard Madame's piano begin at two minutes to eleven by my kitchen clock. It was Chopin. Madame plays Chopin when she is thinking about something she will not say. We heard it stop at eleven minutes past eleven by my kitchen clock.

MATTHEY: You are certain of those readings?

ROSA: Monsieur, I have told you, I am certain of the quarter hour. I have lived by that clock for years.

MATTHEY: Go on, please.

ROSA: I heard the hall clock strike eleven when my kitchen clock showed thirteen minutes past eleven by my kitchen clock. The old Morbier, in the hall, strikes by its own face. I thought, the house is quiet, the master will be pleased with the glasses.

MATTHEY: Later, you went upstairs.

ROSA: Ja. It was nearly the toast. The master likes to be fetched, he does not like to be called from the kitchen like a dog. Up there, Monsieur, he was on the floor by his bench. He was dead. Anyone could see it. I did not touch him. Then I screamed, Herrgott, I screamed.

MATTHEY: Take a moment.

ROSA: I have had my moment. I do not need another.

MATTHEY: Is there anything you noticed in the house tonight that seemed wrong to you, even something small?

ROSA: Only the master's watch. He made everyone show theirs at dinner, as he does every year, and he laughed at Monsieur Félix's father's silver watch. Monsieur Félix did not like it. I was in and out with the plates. I do not know how to say more than that.

MATTHEY: Thank you. You are doing well.

ROSA: Monsieur, are you going to take me to the police post? I have never been inside one. My cousin says they keep you standing.

MATTHEY: Nobody is being taken anywhere tonight. I only need your answers.

ROSA: Then you have them. Madame has been good to me for longer than I can say, and I will answer you about anything, so long as it does not hurt her.

MATTHEY: That is all for now. Thank you, Mademoiselle Häfeli.

ROSA: Ja. Thank you, Monsieur. Somebody should eat something in this house tonight.
